name: Erik Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Erik, I'm 27, and I've worked on the Garrett farm out on Mill Road since I was nineteen. It's a mixed place, but the money is in vegetables for a supermarket contract, and I'm one of the people who makes that contract happen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In season I'm on the tractor by six, lifting carrots or leeks, and the trailers go straight to the packhouse so they can make the supermarket's lorry at four. If the leeks are a centimetre too short or the carrots are bent, the supermarket rejects them, and we plough perfectly good food back into the ground. In winter it's quieter: I feed our sixty suckler cows, fix fences and grease the old Massey Ferguson I've driven for six years. I like the cows and the early light, but the supermarket's rule book wears me out more than the work does.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home with you, and how are you getting by?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lena works nights at a care home, so some weeks we just pass each other on the stairs. Honestly, we're always one boiler repair away from trouble. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank, and the next farm job round here is forty minutes' drive away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So a lot of noise and then not much. I can believe that one, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say in the canteen now: it was always about the bosses selling something. The packhouse got a fancy camera grader two years ago and the supermarket still rings up to reject loads, so where's the magic?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but not happy, because the real problem never goes away. The supermarket keeps squeezing the price per tonne, Mr Garrett keeps squeezing us, and AI or no AI, my pay stays at the bottom of the scale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on doing the job I know. I'd keep going to the farmworkers' union meetings in town, the second Tuesday of the month, and push for the pay claim we've been talking about for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, like being told the bus you didn't want to catch has been cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal week look like for you a few years into that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be working harvest twelve-hour days for the same rate. The difference is this. Nobody gets to say a robot is coming as a way to keep our wages down, which they do say now, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's fine, nothing's changing. She'd laugh, because she knows I don't trust anything I can't fix with a spanner.

S0.say: I'd tell people the AI talk was always the bosses selling something. The packhouse grader came in and the supermarket still rejects loads, so nothing magic happened.
S0.think: I'd be relieved but not happy, because the real squeeze never stops. The supermarket presses the price, the farm presses us, and my pay stays at the bottom either way.
S0.do: Carries on driving and harvesting on the Garrett farm as he does now. Keeps going to the monthly farmworkers' union meetings and pushes the long-running pay claim.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat. Nothing gets worse, but nothing gets better either.
S0.quote: Nobody gets to say a robot is coming as a way to keep our wages down, which they do say now, quietly.
S0.fieldNote: Erik reads AI mainly as a threat bosses use in pay talks, not as a technology. Even in the calmest picture his anger is aimed at the supermarket contract and low pay. He has never used an AI tool and sees no reason to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds more like what's really coming, if I'm honest. I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the workers need a say in how these machines come in, full stop. I'd post the union's line on the farmworkers' group chat: retraining paid by the companies, no sackings without notice, and a share of the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the carrot harvest is the first thing to go. A self-driving harvester with a camera doesn't need me on it, and Mr Garrett would take a cheap lease on one the minute the supermarket asked for a lower price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and get the branch to ask Mr Garrett for a written agreement about machines. I wouldn't buy anything or change anything myself until I saw what he actually does, because I'm not going to retrain for a job that might not exist either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing a noise in the engine and knowing you'll have to look at it eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the two lads from the packhouse, Tomasz and Dev, because grading is already half done by the camera. And the seasonal pickers, who've got no contract at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the harvest goes first, but you also said you'd wait. Isn't that a risky place to wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, that's not a plan. I suppose that's it. My plan is the union, because on my own I've got nothing to bargain with, not even savings.

S1.say: I'd say workers need a say in how the machines come in, with retraining paid by the companies and no sackings without notice. I'd share the union's line in the farmworkers' group chat.
S1.think: I think the carrot harvest is the first job to go, because a self-driving harvester doesn't need me. Mr Garrett would lease one the minute the supermarket pushed the price down.
S1.do: Gets the union branch to ask his boss for a written agreement on new machines. Holds off on retraining or spending anything until he sees what the farm actually does.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a noise in the engine he knows he'll have to deal with.
S1.quote: My plan is the union, because on my own I've got nothing to bargain with, not even savings.
S1.fieldNote: He names the exact job that goes first, his own seat on the harvester, yet won't act alone. When I pointed out the gap, he was honest: his only strength is numbers, because he has no savings. His concern for the packhouse workers and pickers came quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two harvests. That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest robbery in history if the owners of the machines keep all of it. I'd be at the protest, I'd be writing to our representative, and I'd be saying it loud on the chat: tax the robots and pay the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm out of a job before Lena and I have even paid off the car. A robot doesn't need to be cheaper than me by much, and with two weeks of savings I can't wait out anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union and to any campaign for a basic income, an income the government pays everyone. I'd cut everything, the car, the phone contract, the takeaways on Friday, and I'd sign on for whatever help there is the day the notice comes. I wouldn't retrain, because what for, in two years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry underneath it. I'd be lying awake listening to Lena's car come in at seven in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bill goes first, in that first bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, because the cottage belongs to the farm. If I lose the job, we lose the house the same month, and that's what really keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets and the tech companies, and the government that lets them. Not Mr Garrett really, he'd be squeezed too, but he'd still sell my job before his land.

S2.say: I'd call it the biggest robbery in history if the machine owners keep everything. I'd be at the protest and on the group chat saying tax the robots and pay the people.
S2.think: I think I'm out of work within two harvests, with no savings to wait it out. The cottage belongs to the farm, so losing the job means losing our home the same month.
S2.do: Joins union action and any basic income campaign straight away and writes to his representative. Sells or cuts the car, the phone contract and Friday takeaways, and claims public support as soon as notice comes.
S2.feel: Frightened, with anger underneath. He imagines lying awake waiting for Lena to come home from nights.
S2.quote: If I lose the job, we lose the house the same month, and that's what really keeps me up.
S2.fieldNote: The tied cottage, a home that comes with the job, turns job loss into homelessness for him, which is the real fear here. With only two years' warning, he rules out retraining entirely and puts all his energy into politics and public support. He blames supermarkets, tech firms and government, but spares his boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit of breathing room, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but with more time to organise. I'd be saying we need laws now, before it lands, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough for me to waste it. I know myself. I'd tell myself there's time and keep driving the Massey until the day the notice comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put fifty a month away, which is hard, but it would be something. I'd help the union build a list of every farm worker in the district so we could act together when it comes. Lena keeps saying I should look at care work, and maybe in year three or four I'd do the course, but I'd be dragging my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning to anxious. More time sounds better but it also means more time to dread it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first two years look like, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years, I'd mostly be going to meetings and getting people's numbers. A lot of the lads won't join anything until it's too late, so somebody has to do the boring part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years better than two for you, or just different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is worse in one way. With two, there's no choice. With five, it's my fault if I don't move, and I'm not good at moving.

S3.say: I'd say we need laws in place now, before it lands, not after. The message is the same as the fast version, but with more time to organise.
S3.think: I know myself, and I'd probably waste the five years because I dig in. Having time makes not moving feel like my own fault, which is harder than having no choice.
S3.do: Tries to save about fifty a month and spends the first two years building a list of every farm worker in the district for the union. Might take a care work course in year three or four, at Lena's urging, but reluctantly.
S3.feel: Uneasy turning to anxious. Extra time feels like extra time to dread it.
S3.quote: With two, there's no choice. With five, it's my fault if I don't move, and I'm not good at moving.
S3.fieldNote: More warning time doesn't comfort Erik; it adds guilt, because he knows he resists change. He puts his effort into organising other workers rather than his own plan. Care work, his partner's field, is the only switch he names, and he names it reluctantly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a different life by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to make sure the gains get shared, so there's no excuse. I'd be pushing for public retraining money and for the union to get a seat when farms bring in robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels long enough that I could do something real. Maybe I could even be one of the people who fixes the machines, though I've never touched a computer program in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the farm for now, but in the next couple of years I'd ask the college in town about a farm machinery course, evenings, if the union can get it paid. I'd keep saving, even a little, and we'd hold off on having kids until we know where we'd live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but still uneasy. It feels like seeing weather coming over the hill when you've still got time to get the bales in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned holding off on kids. Is that something you and Lena have talked about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, we'd want kids at some point. But not in a cottage that belongs to a farm that might not need me in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think you could learn to fix the machines, when you said you don't trust anything you can't fix with a spanner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of years ago Mr Garrett bought an autosteer kit for the tractor, the thing that steers by satellite. I hated it, but after a month I'd stopped thinking about it. So maybe ten years is enough even for me.

S4.say: I'd say there's a decade to make sure the gains get shared, so nobody has an excuse. I'd push for public retraining money and a union seat whenever farms bring in robots.
S4.think: Ten years might be long enough for even me to change, maybe into fixing the machines. I hated the satellite steering on the tractor and forgot about it within a month.
S4.do: Stays on the farm but asks the town college about an evening farm machinery course in the next two years, hoping the union can fund it. Keeps saving a little and puts off having children until housing is secure.
S4.feel: Uneasy but calmer, like seeing weather on the hill with time to get the bales in.
S4.quote: It feels like seeing weather coming over the hill when you've still got time to get the bales in.
S4.fieldNote: Only the ten-year picture moves Erik from defending his job to planning a new one. The memory of the autosteer kit gave him a small piece of proof that he can adapt. Family plans are tied to the farm cottage, so housing shapes his choices as much as work does.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. What would help is simple: a law that you can't be thrown out of a farm cottage the same month you lose the job, and a union with real teeth when the machines arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the supermarkets. Everyone talks about robots, but it's the supermarket price that decides whether a robot is worth buying, so that's where the real fight is.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thanks. I didn't think I'd talk this much.

headlineQuote: If I lose the job, we lose the house the same month, and that's what really keeps me up.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old tractor driver and stockman on a mixed farm whose income comes mostly from vegetables grown for a supermarket contract. He lives with his partner Lena in a cottage that belongs to the farm, with about two weeks of savings. A committed union member who has never used an AI tool, he reads every scenario through pay, power and the supermarket's grip on prices. He stays calm when AI fizzles out, retreats into union action under gradual change, and is alarmed by the two-year version because losing his job would mean losing his home. Only the ten-year picture gets him thinking about retraining as a machinery technician.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because losing his job would mean losing the farm cottage in the same month.
whatWouldHelp: A law protecting farm workers from losing a tied home the same month as the job, and a union with real power when machines arrive.
